title: A Race for David's Throne
overview: As King David lies close to death, his son Adonijah tries to make himself king, but the prophet Nathan and Solomon's mother Bathsheba move David to have Solomon crowned first.

parts.label: David grows frail (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: The once mighty king can no longer keep warm, so a young woman named Abishag from the town of Shunem is brought in to care for him. The remark that he did not sleep with her seems meant to show how weak he has become, and her place in the royal household matters again in the next chapter.

parts.label: Adonijah claims the crown (vv. 5-10)
parts.note: Adonijah, apparently David's oldest living son, gathers chariots and runners just as his brother Absalom once did, and David, who had never corrected him, says nothing. His large sacrificial feast at a spring outside Jerusalem works like a coronation party, with the army chief Joab and the priest Abiathar on his side and Solomon and those loyal to him left out.

parts.label: Nathan and Bathsheba act (vv. 11-27)
parts.note: A new king often killed rival heirs and their families, so for Bathsheba and Solomon this was life or death. The oath to Solomon that she reminds David of is not mentioned anywhere earlier in Samuel or Kings, so readers differ on whether it was a real past promise or a well timed push on a failing old man.

parts.label: David names Solomon (vv. 28-40)
parts.note: David rouses himself and orders a rival public coronation: Solomon rides the king's own mule, a clear sign of royal approval, and is anointed at the Gihon spring with holy oil from the sacred tent, the rite that publicly set apart Israel's kings. Trumpets and cheering crowds make the choice impossible to ignore.

parts.label: The news reaches the feast (vv. 41-49)
parts.note: Adonijah's guests hear the uproar from the city, and the messenger Jonathan reports that Solomon is already on the throne and that David has blessed it. The guests rise in alarm and scatter.

parts.label: Adonijah at the altar (vv. 50-53)
parts.note: The altar had horn-shaped corners, and holding onto them was a way of claiming sanctuary, a place of protection from being killed. Solomon spares him only on condition of good behavior, a fragile truce that the next chapter tests.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether the chapter mainly shows God's chosen king rising through human scheming, or whether the storyteller is quietly exposing the palace maneuvering that put Solomon on the throne.
think: When a leader is fading, who should get to decide what comes next, and how much does the way a decision is made matter compared with how it turns out?
